title: Container Classes and std::initializer_list
summary: A **container class** holds and manages a collection, like a small `std::vector` of your own. Building one brings together the whole milestone: heap memory, RAII, the Rule of Five and operators. `std::initializer_list` lets it accept `{ 1, 2, 3 }`.
ideas:
1. Type in `IntArray` and add a print statement to every special member function. Check which run for each kind of use.
2. Add an `m_capacity` member with growth by doubling, then `insert(index, value)` and `erase(index)`.
3. After [[9.01 Class Templates]], turn it into a template `DynArray<T>`.

cards.q: Why can one `operator=(IntArray other)` handle both copy and move assignment?
cards.a:
The parameter is copied or moved, depending on the argument

The caller's argument decides how `other` is built. The body is the same swap either way.

cards.q: What does a class need for a range-based `for` loop to work on it?
cards.a:
`begin()` and `end()` functions that return iterators

The range-based `for` calls `begin()` and `end()`. For an array-backed class, pointers to the first and one-past-last elements will do.

Braces would pick the `initializer_list` constructor

Braces prefer an `initializer_list` constructor when there is one, so `{ size }` means "the list containing `size`".

cards.q: Why is this `push_back` slow compared with `std::vector`'s?
cards.a:
It reallocates and copies everything on every call

Growing by one each time makes n insertions cost O(n²). Doubling the capacity makes the average `push_back` constant time.
